title: From Halicarnassus to Thurii: the Inquiry, and the Limit at Elephantine
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: Halicarnassus, the Carian Port That Answers to the King

stops.name: Halicarnassus, birth in a city that pays the King
stops.date_confidence: The Halicarnassian origin is attested in the work's own first line, verified verbatim in the Macaulay translation from Project Gutenberg ebook 2707: 'This is the Showing forth of the Inquiry of Herodotus of Halicarnassos.' The date is not attested at all. 484 is a modern back-calculation from later testimonia running through Pamphila and Aulus Gellius, and the proposals in circulation range across 490 to 480. Month and day are ordering devices. A rival ancient reading of that same opening line gives 'of Thurii' instead; it is handled at its own stop below and is not silently merged here.
stops.campa: A son is born at Halicarnassus, a Dorian foundation on the Carian coast where Greek and Carian names sit in the same family registers and the whole city answers to the Great King. The port looks west across the water toward Cos and Kalymnos; the land behind it is a satrapy. He will begin his book by naming this place, and the naming is the only thing about his birth that any document records. The year 484 is a back-calculation, run through Pamphila and Aulus Gellius by men writing centuries after he was dead. The proposals in circulation range from 490 to 480.
stops.quote: This is the Showing forth of the Inquiry of Herodotus of Halicarnassos, to the end that neither the deeds of men may be forgotten by lapse of time, nor the works great and marvellous, which have been produced some by Hellenes and some by Barbarians, may lose their renown; and especially that the causes may be remembered for which these waged war with one another.
stops.quote_source: Herodotus, Histories 1.1, the proem, tr. G. C. Macaulay, via Wikisource and Project Gutenberg ebook 2707
suggested_refs: The modern statue of Herodotus at Bodrum, Turkey, standing on the site of Halicarnassus; sculptor and installation date not established from any source checked

stops.name: Halicarnassus, the ships sail for Xerxes
stops.date_confidence: Attested in the text itself. Halicarnassus's contribution to the King's fleet is at Histories 7.99 and Artemisia's conduct at Salamis at 8.87 to 8.93. The date is the campaign date and is secure; Herodotus's own age in that year depends entirely on the unattested birth date and cannot be fixed. The stop belongs to the city's own history rather than to any movement of the traveller.
stops.campa: The city sends ships to the King's fleet under its own ruler, Artemisia, daughter of Lygdamis, who sails with them and fights at Salamis in person. He is a small child in the year they go. When he comes to write the war down, decades later, the account he gives of her is close and openly admiring, in a book whose Greek readers have every reason to want her diminished. Halicarnassus is on the Persian side of the Persian Wars, and the man who becomes that war's principal historian is born a subject of the King who lost it.
suggested_refs: Histories 7.99 and 8.87 to 8.93, the Artemisia material, unusually sustained for a commander on the losing side
sources: Herodotus, Histories 7.99, 8.87-93, per standard scholarly summary

stops.name: Halicarnassus, the house of Lyxes
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction from one late source. The Suda, entry eta 536, confirmed verbatim at Suda On Line: 'Son of Lyxes and Dryo; of Halicarnassus... he had a brother [called] Theodoros.' The Suda is tenth-century, roughly fourteen centuries after the events. The working notes for this file gave the entry number as eta.1274, which is wrong; eta 536 is the Herodotus entry. The variant maternal name 'Rhoio' is not a manuscript variant of eta 536 at all: it comes from a different Suda entry, pi 248 on Panyassis, which names 'Rhoea, Herodotus's mother.' Both readings are recorded here and neither is preferred. The date is an ordering device only.
stops.campa: The names of the household come down in a single Byzantine dictionary entry: Lyxes the father, Dryo the mother, Theodorus the brother. A second entry in the same dictionary calls the mother Rhoea instead. Lyxes is a Carian name, not a Greek one, and the boy grows up in a house where two languages and two sets of ancestors are ordinary domestic furniture. Of property, trade, rank, or what any of them did for a living, nothing survives. A father's name, a mother's name under dispute, a brother's name. The entry runs to a line and a half.
suggested_refs: Suda On Line, entries eta 536 (Herodotos) and pi 248 (Panyassis), the whole of the family record
sources: Suda, entry eta 536, via Suda On Line
Suda, entry pi 248, via Suda On Line

stops.name: Halicarnassus, Panyassis in the house
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. The kinship rests on the Suda tradition, which makes Panyassis either uncle or cousin to Herodotus and does not settle which. Panyassis's authorship of a Heracleia and an Ionica is attested in the ancient catalogues; the ranking among the canonical epic poets is a later critical judgement, not a fifth-century one. No fifth-century source connects the two men. Date orders the segment.
stops.campa: A kinsman of the house, Panyassis, is writing epic in an age that has largely stopped producing it: a Heracleia in fourteen books on the labours, and an Ionica on the founding of the Ionian cities. Later critics rank him among the canonical epic poets; no fifth-century source connects the two men. In Halicarnassus he is a relative who works in hexameter. The boy grows up inside the sound of it: fourteen books, recited at family length, on where peoples came from and what they did to each other.
suggested_refs: The fragments of Panyassis of Halicarnassus, Heracleia and Ionica
sources: Suda tradition, via secondary scholarly summary

stops.name: Samos, the island and the dialect
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction resting on a single tenth-century source. Suda eta 536, verbatim: 'He resettled in Samos because of Lygdamis... In Samos he practised the Ionian dialect.' The subject there is Herodotus alone; the fleeing family that appears in modern summaries is an embellishment with no basis in the entry. No fifth-century source confirms exile, residence, or return. Fifth-century inscriptions from Halicarnassus itself are cut in Ionic, which undercuts the entry's own premise that the dialect had to be learned abroad. The coordinates are the Heraion of Samos at 37.67194, 26.88556 per Wikipedia; the working notes gave 37.6892, 26.8825, about 1.9 km north in the plain, and that pin has been dropped. Date orders the segment.
stops.campa: The Byzantine notice says only this: he resettled in Samos because of Lygdamis, and in Samos he practised the Ionian dialect. Later summaries add a fleeing family and a boy carried out of danger; the entry itself has neither, and its premise does not hold either, since the inscriptions cut at Halicarnassus in his own century are already Ionic. What Samos is, is a rich island a day's sail north of home, with a temple of Hera whose successive rebuildings are the largest Greek building project of the age, and a harbour full of men who have been everywhere.
suggested_refs: The fifth-century Ionic inscriptions of Halicarnassus, which contradict the Suda's premise
sources: Suda, entry eta 536, via Suda On Line

stops.name: Samos, the tunnel driven through the mountain
stops.date_confidence: The passage is attested and was confirmed verbatim: Histories 3.60 gives the three greatest works of any Greek land, the tunnel through a mountain one hundred and fifty fathoms high, the harbour mole, and the temple of Hera. The text contains no first-person formula for the tunnel, so personal inspection is probable rather than stated. Coordinates are the Tunnel of Eupalinos at 37.694, 26.930 per Wikipedia; the working notes gave 26.9758, about 4 km too far east, into the hills beyond Pythagoreio, and that longitude has been dropped. Date orders the segment.
stops.campa: He gives Samos more space than its size warrants and says why: the Samians have made three of the greatest works to be seen in any Greek land. A mole thrown out into twenty fathoms of water round the harbour. A temple of Hera larger than any other. And a tunnel bored clean through the base of a mountain a hundred and fifty fathoms high, driven from both ends at once so that water from a spring on the far side reaches the town. The engineer he names by father and by city: Eupalinos son of Naustrophos, a Megarian.
stops.quote: and the designer of this work was a Megarian, Eupalinos the son of Naustrophos
stops.quote_source: Herodotus, Histories 3.60, tr. G. C. Macaulay
suggested_refs: The Tunnel of Eupalinos on Mount Kastro, Samos, driven from both ends and meeting in the middle

stops.name: Halicarnassus, Panyassis killed and the tyrant put down
stops.date_confidence: Two late claims, both from the Suda, neither confirmed by any fifth-century source. The killing is stated flatly at Suda pi 248: 'He was killed by Lygdamis, third tyrant of Halicarnassus.' The Suda gives no motive; the political opposition supplied in modern summaries is a gloss. The return, the part in the overthrow, and the second departure out of unpopularity come from eta 536 and rest on it alone. The whole episode follows the conventional biographical shape of an anti-tyrannical intellectual's life, which is a reason for caution and not a reason for rejection. Date is an ordering device; nothing dates any of it.
stops.campa: Lygdamis the third tyrant kills Panyassis. The entry that records it gives no reason, and every motive since supplied has been supplied by moderns. The other tradition says Herodotus came back, took part in putting the tyrant down, and then found himself disliked by his fellow citizens and left of his own accord. No fifth-century source knows anything about any of this. Did he leave as a defeated partisan, as a disliked victor, or for something nobody thought to write down? The entry does not say. He does not stay.
suggested_refs: Suda, entries pi 248 and eta 536, the sole authority for the whole Lygdamis episode
sources: Suda, entries pi 248 and eta 536, via Suda On Line

segments.name: The King's Roads: Lydia, the Straits, and the Phoenician Shore

stops.name: Sardis, the burnt temple and the Lydian kings
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction as to the visit; the topographical detail is close enough that scholarship treats intimate knowledge of western Anatolia as probable personal experience, but no itinerary statement covers Sardis. The chapter reference in the working notes was off by one: 5.101 gives the burning of the city, the reed houses, the agora and the Pactolus, while the temple appears at 5.102, 'Sardis was then destroyed by fire, and in it also the temple of the native goddess Hybebe.' The Solon and Croesus interview is at 1.29 to 1.33 and is a set piece, not a report. Coordinates match Wikipedia's Sardis to within about 360 m. Date orders the segment.
stops.campa: Sardis is the satrapal seat of Lydia and the western end of the King's road, a city of reed-roofed houses along the Pactolus where the gold comes down out of the hills. He knows its market and its river, and he knows what happened to it: burned in the Ionian Revolt, and the temple of the native goddess burned with it, which is the injury Persia afterwards gives as its reason for coming to Greece. Here he stages the interview in which an Athenian lawgiver tells the richest king alive that no man can be counted happy while he still has time to lose it.
stops.quote: Call him, however, until he die, not happy but fortunate.
stops.quote_source: Herodotus, Histories 1.32, Solon to Croesus, tr. George Rawlinson, via classics.mit.edu
suggested_refs: The temple of Cybebe at Sardis, burned in the Ionian Revolt, cited by Persia as cause for the invasion of Greece

stops.name: The Bosporus at Chalcedon, the sea measured in sailing days
stops.date_confidence: The measurements at Histories 4.85 to 4.86 are attested; the confident language attributed to them in the working notes is not. The text does not say 'exactly ascertained': 4.86 reads 'These measurements I have made as follows: a ship completes on an average in a long day a distance of seventy thousand fathoms,' an arithmetic estimate from sailing time, not a survey. The Macaulay text prints a dash after that colon, silently dropped in the quote field here. The Hieron does not appear in the passage at all; 4.85 puts Darius's bridge of boats in the territory of Chalcedon and puts Darius himself at the Kyanean rocks to look at the Pontus. The working notes' pin at 41.1913, 29.0898 sits between the two and matches neither, and has been dropped for Chalcedon, modern Kadikoy. Date orders the segment.
stops.campa: He gives the Pontus a length and a breadth, the Bosporus a width, the Hellespont a run, and the Propontis a size, in fathoms, to the figure. Then he shows his working, which almost nobody in antiquity does: a ship makes seventy thousand fathoms in a long day and sixty thousand in a night, so many days across is so many fathoms. It is arithmetic, not survey. The strait itself he treats as the place where Darius laid a bridge of boats over from the Chalcedonian side and then sailed up to the rocks at the mouth to look at the water he had just made into a road.
stops.quote: These measurements I have made as follows: a ship completes on an average in a long day a distance of seventy thousand fathoms
stops.quote_source: Herodotus, Histories 4.86, tr. G. C. Macaulay
suggested_refs: The Kyanean rocks at the mouth of the Bosporus, where 4.85 places Darius looking out over the Pontus

stops.name: Abydos, the strait that was whipped
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction as to any visit. Histories 7.33 to 7.37 narrates the double pontoon bridge and the flogging of the Hellespont in vivid detail, and the events belong to 480, decades before any research journey of his. There is no first-person claim for the site. The date here places him at the crossing during the research years as an ordering device; the text does not assert that he was ever there.
stops.campa: At the narrowest crossing between Asia and Europe, Xerxes has his engineers lash two bridges of boats from shore to shore, and a storm takes them out. The King orders the sea given three hundred lashes and a pair of fetters thrown into it, and the men who built the first bridges beheaded. Then it is built again, twice over, on cables of flax and papyrus. He never says he saw the place, and he tells it with a surveyor's attention to the width, the cables, the anchorage. The army crosses for seven days and seven nights without stopping.
suggested_refs: Histories 7.33-37, the bridging of the Hellespont, told with measurements and no autopsy claim
sources: Herodotus, Histories 7.33-37, per standard scholarly summary

stops.name: Sestos, where the narrative stops running
stops.date_confidence: The ending is attested: Histories 9.114 to 9.122. The working notes said the work closes on the impaling of Artayctes; it does not. Artayctes is nailed to boards at 9.120 and the final chapter is 9.122, Cyrus's maxim that soft lands breed soft men. Coordinates are Wikipedia's Sestos at 40.23278, 26.4225; the working notes' 40.2064, 26.3903 sits about 3.4 km southwest and has been dropped. Whether Herodotus visited the Chersonese is nowhere stated; the date is an ordering device.
stops.campa: On the European shore opposite, the Athenians besiege the last Persian-held town in Europe and take it in the year after Salamis. The governor Artayctes, who had plundered the shrine of Protesilaus, is nailed to boards on the headland and his son stoned to death in front of him. This is where the nine books stop running. Not on the impaling, which is chapter one hundred and twenty, but two chapters further on, with an old exchange about rugged countries breeding rugged men, and then nothing: no summary, no return to the author, no last word.
suggested_refs: Histories 9.114-122, the closing chapters, ending on Cyrus's maxim rather than on the execution

stops.name: Tyre, the temple of the god the Greeks call Heracles
stops.date_confidence: Attested and among the most widely accepted of his claimed destinations. Histories 2.44 presents the visit as autopsy: he says he sailed to Tyre for the purpose of the inquiry and describes the temple's two pillars, one gold and one of a stone that shone at night. The figure of some two thousand three hundred years is local priestly tradition reported as such, not verified chronology, and scholarship treats it that way. Date orders the segment.
stops.campa: He sails to Phoenicia for one reason: to settle how old Heracles is. The priests in the temple at Tyre tell him the sanctuary was founded when the city was founded, two thousand three hundred years back, which runs further back than anything Greek tradition claims for the same god. He does not correct the figure and he does not swallow it; he writes down what they said and marks it as theirs. Of the place itself he records two pillars, one of gold and one of a green stone that shines all night.
suggested_refs: Histories 2.44, the Tyre inquiry, one of the clearest autopsy statements outside Book 2's Egyptian chapters
sources: Herodotus, Histories 2.44, via Penelope/Thayer text of the Histories

stops.name: Babylon, the walls and the tower of Bel
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction, and the most contested travel question in the whole of Herodotean scholarship. Histories 1.178 to 1.183 describes the walls, the gates, the tiered tower of Bel and the golden statue; genuine information sits beside errors of a kind a visitor should not make, and whether he ever reached the city is disputed rather than settled. This file takes no side. Coordinates are inherited byte for byte from the canonical Babylon pin already used at cyrus.journey.json, ctesias.journey.json and nabucodonosor_ii.journey.json. Date is an ordering device.
stops.campa: He gives the city a square of wall so long that no army could man it, a hundred gates of bronze, and at the centre a tower in eight stages with a way running up the outside of it and a great seated figure of gold in the temple below. He tells how Cyrus took the place by turning the Euphrates aside and walking his men up the drained riverbed while the city was keeping a festival and did not know the outer quarters had fallen. Whether he ever stood in front of any of it is the longest-running argument in the reading of him.
suggested_refs: Ctesias of Cnidus, Persica, twenty-three books written expressly against Herodotus on Persian and Babylonian matters, from inside the Achaemenid court a generation later
sources: Modern scholarly debate on the Babylon visit, per standard reference works

segments.name: Egypt, from the Delta to the First Cataract

stops.name: Naucratis, the Greek town in the Delta
stops.date_confidence: The description at Histories 2.178 to 2.179 is attested, including Amasis's grant and the cities that jointly founded the Hellenion. There is no first-person visit claim for Naucratis itself; as the standard port of entry for Greeks into Egypt a stop here is inferred rather than stated. The customs material quoted is from 2.35 and was fetched directly from the Rawlinson text. The Egyptian journey as a whole is accepted by most scholars and is conventionally placed in the 450s or 440s, but that dating has no ancient anchor and the year here is an estimate used to order the segment.
stops.campa: Amasis gave the Greeks this town on the Canopic branch, and the cities of Ionia and Doris and Aeolis built the Hellenion in it jointly, so this is where a Greek enters Egypt and where his interpreters are found. What he reports from the country beyond begins as a catalogue of inversions. The women go to market and trade; the men sit at home at the loom. The rest of the world works the weft up the warp and the Egyptians work it down. Women carry their loads on the shoulder, men carry theirs on the head.
stops.quote: the people also, in most of their manners and customs, exactly reverse the common practice of mankind.
stops.quote_source: Herodotus, Histories 2.35, tr. George Rawlinson, via classics.mit.edu
suggested_refs: The Hellenion at Naucratis, founded jointly by the Ionian, Dorian and Aeolian cities named at Histories 2.178

stops.name: The Canopic mouth, the boats built like courses of brick
stops.date_confidence: The description of the Nile cargo boat, the baris, is Herodotus's own at Histories 2.96 and is attested. The pin is not: Herodotus names no town here. The coordinates are Thonis-Heracleion, the drowned port at the Canopic mouth, given by Wikipedia as 31.31278, 30.12889; the working notes' 31.3, 30.1667 sits about 3.7 km southeast and has been dropped. The pin is an editorial placement at the river mouth every Greek entering Egypt used, chosen because the hull known as Ship 17, excavated there by Franck Goddio's IEASM team between 2009 and 2011, was found to match this construction. That finding was reported in March 2019, in the Guardian of 17 March; the January 2019 date in the working notes is unsupported and no journal or month is named in the underlying citation.
stops.campa: The Nile cargo boats are built in a way no Greek yard builds, and he sets the method down the way a man sets down something he has watched being loaded. Planks of acacia cut about three feet long and laid like courses of brickwork, pinned through with long dowels, the seams caulked with papyrus, a single steering oar driven down through the keel. Going downstream they hang a hurdle of tamarisk ahead of the bow and drag a holed stone behind, so that the current pulls the hurdle forward and the stone keeps the hull straight.
suggested_refs: Ship 17 at Thonis-Heracleion, excavated 2009-2011, whose hull construction was matched to the baris of Histories 2.96 and reported in March 2019
sources: Dalya Alberge, 'Nile shipwreck discovery proves Herodotus right,' The Guardian, 17 March 2019

stops.name: Sais, the lake and the rites he will not describe
stops.date_confidence: Attested at Histories 2.170 as first-person knowledge withheld: he describes the precinct and the nocturnal rites on the lake and states that he knows the full account and will not divulge it. The declared discretion is read by standard scholarship as evidence of presence and of admission to informants, not as a rhetorical pose, though it cannot be tested either way. Date orders the segment.
stops.campa: In the precinct of the goddess at Sais there is a tomb behind the temple, and he declines to give the name of the one who lies in it, though he says he knows it. On a lake nearby, at night, the Egyptians perform what they call the mysteries, acting out that same god's sufferings by torchlight. He says he knows the whole account of these things as well, and then stops. A foreigner has been let far enough into a sanctuary to be told what he must not repeat. He does not repeat it.
suggested_refs: Histories 2.170-171, the withheld name and the night rites on the lake at Sais

stops.name: Buto, the island he watched and it did not move
stops.date_confidence: Attested at Histories 2.155 to 2.156, and among the clearest autopsy-style statements in Book 2: he describes the temple and oracle of Leto at Buto and the island of Chemmis, and states plainly that he never saw the island float or move at all. The negative testimony is the strong part of the evidence here, since a fabricator has no reason to report a marvel failing to occur. Date orders the segment.
stops.campa: At Buto stands the oracle of Leto, and beside it, the Egyptians say, an island called Chemmis that floats and moves about the lake, carrying a temple of Apollo and a grove of palms, where Leto hid the child from Typhon. He goes and looks. The oracle he takes seriously, and lists among the ones the Egyptians hold truest. Of the island he writes that he himself never saw it move or float at all, and that he was astonished to hear an island could do any such thing.
suggested_refs: Histories 2.155-156, the oracle of Leto and the island of Chemmis that he watched and that did not move

stops.name: Heliopolis, the same question asked twice
stops.date_confidence: Attested by a direct first-person statement of itinerary and purpose at Histories 2.3, confirmed verbatim: 'I visited Thebes too and Heliopolis for this very purpose, because I desired to know if the people of those places would tell me the same tale.' This is the strongest travel claim in Book 2 after the Elephantine limit at 2.29. The year is an estimate; no ancient source dates the Egyptian journey.
stops.campa: The priests of Heliopolis have the name of being the most learned in Egypt, and he goes to them for what he actually wants out of the country, which is not marvels but chronology: how long the gods reigned, how long the kings after them, in what order, against what Greek reckoning. Then he takes the same questions to Memphis and to Thebes and asks them again, so that the three answers can be set against each other and made to come apart. He says as much in the text: he went to those places to know whether the people there would tell him the same tale.
stops.quote: I visited Thebes too and Heliopolis for this very purpose, because I desired to know if the people of those places would tell me the same tale.
stops.quote_source: Herodotus, Histories 2.3, tr. G. C. Macaulay
suggested_refs: Histories 2.3, the itinerary sentence that names Memphis, Heliopolis and Thebes and states the reason for going to all three

stops.name: Memphis, the priests of Ptah
stops.date_confidence: Attested at Histories 2.3, the same sentence as Heliopolis and Thebes: he reports conversing with the priests of the god he calls Hephaestus, that is Ptah, at Memphis. The Delta-as-alluvium argument is at 2.10 to 2.12 and is his own reasoning, not priestly report. The written king-list is at 2.100 and following. Date orders the segment.
stops.campa: At Memphis he sits with the priests of the god he calls Hephaestus and takes down the Egyptian account of the country's own making: that the first king dammed the river and drained the ground the city stands on, and that the whole Delta below is land the river built out of its own silt. They show him a written list of kings and the count of generations that goes with it. Nothing in Greek memory reaches back anything like so far. He says so, and takes the Egyptian reckoning as the longer and the better of the two.
suggested_refs: Histories 2.10-12, the argument that the Delta is alluvial land, reasoned from silting rather than taken from informants

stops.name: Giza, the pyramids and the labour figures
stops.date_confidence: Attested as text at Histories 2.124 to 2.127, and the level of description implies direct observation of the monuments; the content is another matter. The royal chronology and the attributions conflict badly with Egyptian evidence, and the labour arithmetic is priestly report rather than record. The distinction kept here is between what he saw, which the dimensions suggest he did, and what he was told, which is most of the rest. Date orders the segment.
stops.campa: The priests tell him that Cheops shut the temples, stopped the sacrifices, and put the whole nation to the work: a hundred thousand men at a time relieved every three months, ten years for the causeway that brought the stones up and twenty more for the pyramid itself. The kings he is given and the centuries he assigns them are wrong by a wide margin; the dimensions, which read like the figures of a man pacing out a base, are not. Khafre's stands beside it, built to the same plan, and lower.
suggested_refs: Histories 2.124-127, the construction account, where the dimensions and the chronology come from two different kinds of source
sources: Herodotus, Histories 2.124-127, per standard scholarly summary

stops.name: Hawara, the Labyrinth and the rooms he was not shown
stops.date_confidence: Attested first-person autopsy at Histories 2.148, with the limit of that autopsy stated in the same passage: the upper chambers he was walked through, the lower ones he was only told about. The working notes render the quotation with an ellipsis bridging the two halves; only the first half is used in the quote field here, and the second is given in the campa as reported. Date orders the segment.
stops.campa: Near the lake of Moeris stands a walled building of twelve roofed courts and three thousand chambers, half of them above the ground and half beneath it, and he says the pyramids are beneath it in the reckoning of wonders. He is taken through the upper rooms and walks them: courts opening onto courts, passages turning back through colonnades, roofs of cut stone. The lower half he is not shown. The keepers say the tombs of the kings who built it and of the sacred crocodiles are down there, and will not open them, so of the underground chambers he has only what he was told.
stops.quote: I have myself seen it, and indeed no words can tell its wonders
stops.quote_source: Herodotus, Histories 2.148, tr. G. C. Macaulay
suggested_refs: The Hawara complex beside Lake Moeris, identified with the Labyrinth of Histories 2.148

stops.name: Thebes, the wooden colossi and the generations
stops.date_confidence: The visit is attested in the itinerary sentence at Histories 2.3. The colossi episode is at 2.143, where Herodotus names Hecataeus of Miletus, the earlier Ionian prose writer, and reports the priests counting the statues against Hecataeus's claimed sixteenth-generation descent from a god. Herodotus's engagement with Hecataeus is attested across 2.143, 5.36 and 6.137 and is one of the few cases where he names a predecessor in order to correct him. Date orders the segment.
stops.campa: Far up the river he puts the Heliopolitan questions to the priests of Amun and gets a third version to set beside the other two. In the great precinct they keep wooden statues of the high priests, each one the son of the man before him, standing in a line generation by generation. They had shown the same statues to Hecataeus of Miletus when he came and recited a family tree that reached a god in the sixteenth generation. They counted the colossi at him: three hundred and forty-five men, father to son, and no god at the end of them.
suggested_refs: Histories 2.143, 5.36 and 6.137, where Hecataeus of Miletus is named and corrected
sources: Herodotus, Histories 5.36, 6.137, per standard scholarly summary

stops.name: Elephantine, the limit of his own eyes
stops.date_confidence: Attested, and the clearest textual marker anywhere in the work for the boundary of his personal travel: Histories 2.29, confirmed verbatim, 'By my own travel and sight as far as the city of Elephantine, and beyond that by question and hearsay.' Everything south of this line in Book 2 is explicitly secondhand by his own declaration. The date remains an estimate; the limit does not.
stops.campa: The island in the river at the first cataract is the southern edge of Egypt and the southern edge of what he will claim to have seen. Above it the water breaks over rock and boats must be hauled by rope from the bank. He draws the line here in the text itself: by his own travel and sight as far as Elephantine, and beyond that by question and hearsay. He asks everybody he meets where the Nile begins, and gets one clerk at Sais who says he knows and whom he does not believe, and after that nothing but distances counted in days of travel.
stops.quote: By my own travel and sight as far as the city of Elephantine, and beyond that by question and hearsay.
stops.quote_source: Herodotus, Histories 2.29, tr. G. C. Macaulay
suggested_refs: Histories 2.29, the declared southern limit of autopsy, against which the rest of Book 2 can be tested

segments.name: The Edges: Libya and the Scythian Cold

stops.name: Cyrene, the colony and the silphium
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction as to any visit. Histories 4.145 to 4.205 gives the colonisation traditions, the king-list, the Libyan tribal customs and the silphium in a density of detail that makes a visit to Cyrenaica plausible; no itinerary statement confirms it, and scholarship is clear that he did not cross the Sahara or reach the remoter peoples he describes. Two mutually incompatible foundation stories, the Theran and the Cyrenaean, are set down side by side in the text without adjudication, and are left that way here. Date orders the segment.
stops.campa: He has the whole foundation story in two versions, the Theran and the Cyrenaean, and sets them out side by side without picking one: a stammering man told by the oracle to found a city in Libya, an island that did not want to give up its people, a first site that failed, and then the place with the hole in the sky where the rain comes through. He has the kings after Battus and the wars with Egypt. He has the plant, silphium, that grows along this one strip of coast and nowhere else on earth, and that the city stamps on its coins.
suggested_refs: Histories 4.145-205, the two irreconcilable foundation accounts of Cyrene, printed together

stops.name: West of the Triton, among the Maxyans
stops.date_confidence: The passage is attested and verified verbatim at Histories 4.191 from Macaulay via Project Gutenberg 2707; the placement in the working notes was wrong twice over. The text sets this country west of the river Triton, next after the Auseans, among the Maxyans, not west of the Nasamones, who are an eastern people of the Syrtis described separately at 4.172-190. And the working coordinates of 27 N, 15 E point into the deep central Sahara, whereas Lake Tritonis is conventionally the Chott el-Djerid, which sends the description northwest toward the Tunisian Tell. The pin here is that rough correction and fixes no site: the text names none. Herodotus reports the beings as Libyan speech, with the attribution in the sentence, not as anything he saw.
stops.campa: Past the river Triton the country changes: hills, forest, wild beasts, elephants and lions and bears, and men who plough. The people here, the Maxyans, wear their hair long on the right side and shaved on the left, paint their bodies red, and say they came out of Troy. What lives further in he has from them and not from his own eyes, and he puts the attribution inside the sentence where it cannot come loose: dog-headed men, headless men with their eyes in their chests, wild men and wild women, at least so say the Libyans about them.
stops.quote: the dog-headed men, and the headless men with their eyes set in their breasts (at least so say the Libyans about them), and the wild men and wild women
stops.quote_source: Herodotus, Histories 4.191, tr. G. C. Macaulay, Project Gutenberg ebook 2707
suggested_refs: Ctesias, Indica, and Megasthenes, Indica: the later Greek relocation of the dog-headed men from Libya to India, and the source of the medieval cynocephali
sources: Herodotus, Histories 4.191 (Macaulay, Gutenberg 2707), fetched and verified verbatim
Herodotus, Histories 4.191 (Godley, Loeb 1921), via Wikisource search snippet, page itself not loadable

stops.name: Olbia, the king who worshipped in secret
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction as to the visit, attested as text. The Scythian ethnography of Book 4 centres on the Greek trading zone around Olbia at the Bug and Dnieper estuary, and the Scyles episode is at 4.78 to 4.80. Scholarship judges a visit to this Greek emporion probable; a journey deep into Scythia proper is not demonstrable and is not claimed here. Archaeology of kurgan burial and horse culture corroborates much of the ethnography without touching the question of where he stood. Date orders the segment.
stops.campa: At the trading town by the estuary the Scythian king Scyles keeps a house with Greek furniture and a wife from the town, and every time he brings his army up he leaves it outside the wall, changes his clothes inside the gate, and lives a month at a time as a Greek. Scythians will not take on foreign customs, the story says, and Greek ones least of all. One of his own people is shown him going through the Bacchic rite. The Scythians revolt on the spot. Scyles runs to Thrace, is handed back over the river, and his brother takes his head off.
suggested_refs: Histories 4.78-80, the Scyles episode, told from inside the Greek emporion rather than from the steppe
sources: Archaeological corroboration of the Scythian logos, per modern scholarship summary

stops.name: Exampaeus, the cauldron they made him look at
stops.date_confidence: Attested as first-person autopsy inside the Scythian logos, and the clearest such claim in Book 4: at Histories 4.81 he says the people of the country made him see the bronze bowl for himself, and he gives its capacity and the thickness of its metal. The location of Exampaeus between the Hypanis and the Borysthenes is not resolved on the ground, so the coordinates here are approximate and should not be read as a site identification.
stops.campa: Between the two rivers there is a bitter spring that spoils the whole Hypanis where it runs in, and at that place, which the Scythians call Exampaeus, the people of the country make him look at a bowl. It is the one time in the whole northern account that he says so. Bronze, six fingers thick, holding by his reckoning six hundred amphorae; a king had it cast, they say, out of one arrowhead demanded from every man in Scythia, because he wanted to know how many of them there were.
suggested_refs: Histories 4.81, the Exampaeus cauldron, offered as a census in bronze

segments.name: The Oracles and the Battlefields of Greece

stops.name: Dodona, the three prophetesses named
stops.date_confidence: Attested at Histories 2.54 to 2.57, and unusual in the work because he names his informants: the prophetesses of Dodona, whose account he sets against the Egyptian version he had been given at Thebes. Naming the women strengthens the claim that an inquiry was actually conducted on the site, which is why standard scholarship treats this stop as among the better-evidenced. Date orders the segment.
stops.campa: The priests at Egyptian Thebes told him two holy women were carried off by Phoenicians, one sold into Libya and one into Greece, and that the second founded this oracle. At Dodona he asks the prophetesses and gets the other version: a black dove came out of Egypt, settled in the oak, and spoke with a human voice telling them to make an oracle of Zeus in that place. Two accounts of one shrine, taken in two countries, go into the book unreconciled. He names the three women who gave him the second: Promeneia, Timarete, Nicandra.
suggested_refs: Histories 2.54-57, where the informants at Dodona are named, which happens almost nowhere else in the work

stops.name: Dodona, the gods given their names and their shapes
stops.date_confidence: Attested. The passage is the continuation of the Dodona inquiry and is placed at that pin for that reason: Histories 2.52 has the oracle consulted about whether to adopt the divine names brought out of Egypt, and 2.53 states that Homer and Hesiod made the Greek theogony and lived four hundred years before his own time and no more. Herodotus offers the dating as his own opinion from inquiry, not as anyone's record. The same chapter is cited as attested at homer.journey.json and twice at hesiod.journey.json, where his four-hundred-year figure points to the mid-ninth century and cuts against the conventional dating of both poets. Date orders the segment.
stops.campa: The prophetesses tell him more than the founding story. The Pelasgians once sacrificed to gods with no names at all, calling them only the disposers, and the names came later out of Egypt, and it was this oracle that was asked whether to take them and said yes. As for where the Greek gods got their parentage, their titles, their honours and their shapes: that is the work of Homer and Hesiod, who lived, he reckons, four hundred years before his own time and not more. Two poets, one pantheon, and a date he gives as his own opinion and nobody else's.
suggested_refs: Histories 2.53, whose four-hundred-year figure would put Homer and Hesiod in the mid-ninth century, against the conventional dating of both
sources: Herodotus, Histories 2.52-53, per standard scholarly summary

stops.name: Delphi, the offerings in the treasuries
stops.date_confidence: Attested as description, not as declared autopsy, and the working notes had the treasury wrong. Histories 1.51 puts the golden bowl in the treasury of the people of Clazomenae and the silver one in the corner of the vestibule; it is Gyges's offerings at 1.14 that stand in the treasury the Greeks call the Corinthians', which Herodotus adds is really Kypselos's and not the Corinthian state's. There is no first-person 'I saw' at 1.51: the passage is present-tense description implying autopsy rather than asserting it, so the tag has been softened here. Coordinates inherited byte for byte from the canonical Delphi pin at cyrus.journey.json. The bribed Pythia is at 6.66.
stops.campa: Croesus emptied a treasury into this sanctuary before he lost his kingdom, and the dedications are still standing when Herodotus walks through. A gold bowl among the offerings of the Clazomenians. A silver one in the corner of the entrance hall. Further along, in the building everyone calls the Corinthians' treasury, the offerings of Gyges, and he notes as he passes that the building is not the Corinthian state's at all but the tyrant Kypselos's. He also records, without softening it anywhere, that a Pythia was once bought to give a Spartan king the answer he wanted.
suggested_refs: Histories 1.14 and 1.51, the Lydian dedications, and 6.66, the purchased oracle

stops.name: Olympia, the reading, or else the shade
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction, and two late traditions that contradict each other head on. Lucian, Herodotus or Aetion, second century CE, has him read the whole work aloud at the festival to instant Panhellenic fame; an ancient grammarian, cited without a name in the reference summaries, has him wait for cloud-shade until the audience dispersed, whence the proverb about Herodotus and his shade. Both are recorded centuries after the fact and neither is preferred here. Public performance of parts of the work is plausible on general grounds; a single-sitting recitation of nine books is not. The Muse-titles are a Hellenistic editorial arrangement, not his.
stops.campa: One story has him carry the finished work across from Asia, wait for the festival, read the whole of it aloud in one sitting to the assembled Greeks and walk away famous in every city at once, with the nine books named for the nine Muses on the spot. The other has him waiting at Olympia for a cloud so he would not have to read in the sun, and by the time the shade came the crowd had gone home, which is where the saying about Herodotus and his shade comes from. Both are told centuries later. They cannot both be true and neither one has to be.
suggested_refs: Lucian, Herodotus or Aetion, second century CE, the source of the Olympic triumph legend
sources: Lucian, Herodotus or Aetion, per Wikipedia 'Herodotus'
Wikipedia, 'Herodotus', for the rival shade anecdote attributed to an ancient grammarian

stops.name: Marathon, the mound over the dead
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction as to any visit; the narrative at Histories 6.102 to 6.117 is attested and is the fullest surviving ancient account of the battle. The topographical detail suggests informants on the ground or a visit, but no first-person claim covers the field. The count of a hundred and ninety-two Athenian dead comes from the same chapter range and is followed here as the standard reading. The Soros, the mound on the plain, is a real and excavated monument. Date orders the segment.
stops.campa: The Athenians come down out of the hills into the plain and cover the last stretch at a run, which he says no Greek had done before against Persians, and the line breaks at the wings and holds in the centre. Fifteen chapters carry the fullest account of that day surviving from antiquity, and every later version runs back through them. Their dead, a hundred and ninety-two of them, go under one mound raised on the field where they fell. The mound is still standing on the plain.
suggested_refs: The Soros, the burial mound of the Athenian dead on the plain of Marathon

stops.name: Thermopylae, the path over the ridge
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction as to any visit; the narrative at Histories 7.201 to 7.233 is attested. The specificity of the Anopaea path, where it starts, where it comes out, and how long it takes to walk, points to on-the-ground informants or to a visit, but the text makes no first-person claim for the pass. Date orders the segment.
stops.campa: The pass is a cart-track between cliff and sea with an old wall thrown across it, and for two days a few thousand Greeks hold it against the King's whole army, because numbers cannot be brought to bear in that width. What the account knows best is not the fighting but the ground: where the path over the ridge starts, where it comes out, how long it takes a column to walk. A local man shows the Persians that path and the position is turned in a night. Leonidas sends most of the allies away and stays with the Spartans and the Thespians.
suggested_refs: The Anopaea path over Kallidromon, described in enough detail to be walked

stops.name: Salamis, the strait his own city fought in
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction as to any visit; the narrative at Histories 8.40 to 8.96 is attested and is the principal ancient account of the battle. No autopsy claim is made for the strait. The Halicarnassian contingent under Artemisia is attested at 7.99 and her conduct in the battle at 8.87 to 8.93. Date orders the segment.
stops.campa: Themistocles sends a man across in the dark to tell Xerxes the Greeks mean to slip away, and the Persian fleet closes both exits in the night and rows at dawn into a strait too narrow to use its numbers in. Among the ships fighting on the King's side are those of Halicarnassus, under Artemisia, and the man who will write the battle down never conceals that his own city sent them. The King has a throne set up on the slope opposite, with secretaries beside it writing down who does well and who does not.
suggested_refs: Histories 8.87-93, Artemisia at Salamis, written by a citizen of the city whose ships she commanded

stops.name: Plataea, the last land battle and the grudge it left
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction as to any visit; the tactical narrative at Histories 9.19 to 9.89 is attested. The Theban presence on the Persian side is at 9.31 to 9.32 and is cited as attested at pindar.journey.json for the same fact. The Boeotian rejoinder, Plutarch's On the Malice of Herodotus, is a later treatise and is carried here as a source about the reception of this passage, not as a scene: Plutarch's engagement is his own, five centuries downstream. Date orders the segment.
stops.campa: Mardonius winters in Thessaly and comes down in the spring, and the two armies sit facing each other across the Asopus for eleven days while the sacrifices refuse to come out right for either side. Then the Greek line falls apart in a night withdrawal that goes wrong, and the battle happens anyway, in pieces, on ground nobody had chosen. The Thebans are in the field on the Persian side. He writes that down, and Boeotia does not forgive it: five centuries later a Boeotian writer devotes an entire treatise to proving him malicious.
suggested_refs: Plutarch, On the Malice of Herodotus, the Boeotian answer to Histories 9.31-32, written some five centuries later
sources: Plutarch, On the Malice of Herodotus, per standard scholarly summary

segments.name: The Colony in the West, and Athens

stops.name: Thurii, the new city on the plain of Sybaris
stops.date_confidence: The colony is attested: Thurii was founded in 443 under Athenian sponsorship with Pericles's backing, the colonists led out by Lampon and Xenocritus, on the plain of destroyed Sybaris in southern Italy. Herodotus's inclusion among the original colonists is ancient tradition and is tagged reconstruction, not attested. Coordinates are Wikipedia's Thurii at 39.71722, 16.49556; the working notes' 39.7075, 16.5375 sits about 4 km east, at or past the modern shoreline, and has been dropped.
stops.campa: Athens founds a colony in the west on the plain where Sybaris stood until its neighbours destroyed it sixty years before and whose survivors want it back. It is advertised as Panhellenic: settlers taken from any Greek city that will send them, under Athenian sponsorship, led out by Lampon and Xenocritus. A town built to belong to all the Greeks equally is close to the readership his book is written for, and tradition puts him among the first colonists. Tradition is all there is: no list of settlers survives. The year is 443.
suggested_refs: The Sybaris archaeological park near Sibari, Cosenza, over the site of Thurii
sources: Wikipedia, 'Thurii' (foundation and coordinates), synthesising Diodorus Siculus and other ancient testimony

stops.name: Thurii, the name in the first line
stops.date_confidence: Attested, and stronger than the working notes allowed. Aristotle's Rhetoric 3.9, at 1409a, was fetched directly from Perseus and reads: 'This is the exposition of the investigation of Herodotus of Thurii.' So a fourth-century Athenian text of the proem gave Thurii, while the manuscripts that reach Byzantium give Halicarnassus. Both readings are ancient; neither can be removed. What the variant proves about actual citizenship or permanent residence is inference, judged highly probable rather than certain. The Aristotelian citation is kept in the source apparatus and out of the narrative, per the corpus rule on later engagements.
stops.campa: The book opens by naming its author and his city, and there are two readings of that line. The manuscripts that come down to Byzantium say Halicarnassus. A fourth-century Athenian, quoting the sentence in a treatise on style, gives Thurii instead. Both readings are ancient and neither can be got rid of. Somewhere between the founding of the colony and the copying of the text, the man who began by calling himself a Carian was recorded as calling himself a westerner.
suggested_refs: Aristotle, Rhetoric 3.9 (1409a), the 'of Thurii' reading of the proem, verified by direct fetch of the Perseus text
sources: Aristotle, Rhetoric 1409a, via Perseus Digital Library, fetched directly

stops.name: Athens, the verses Sophocles made
stops.date_confidence: Attested as ancient testimony, disputed as interpretation, and the date in the working notes was wrong. Plutarch, Moralia 785b, An seni respublica gerenda sit, verified verbatim at Thayer's Penelope text: 'Song for Herodotus Sophocles made when the years of his age were Five in addition to fifty.' Sophocles was born c. 497/496, so his fifty-fifth year falls in 442/441; the figure usually printed in the literature is 441/440. The 440/439 given in the working notes is one to two years late and does not follow from the age-55 datum. The poem itself does not survive. This is the strongest surviving evidence of personal contact between the two men and it does not establish a friendship.
stops.campa: A couplet survives, quoted by a writer five centuries downstream, saying that Sophocles made a song for Herodotus in his fifty-fifth year. The song itself is gone. Two lines of a much later quotation are the whole documentary basis for a friendship everyone since has assumed, and what they establish is narrower: that the two men were in the same literary world in the same season, and that one of them wrote something for the other. He is in Athens often enough for its traditions to run all through his book. The Byzantine life of him does not mention Athens at all.
stops.quote: Song for Herodotus Sophocles made when the years of his age were Five in addition to fifty.
stops.quote_source: Plutarch, Moralia 785b, An seni respublica gerenda sit, via Thayer/Penelope
suggested_refs: Plutarch, Moralia 785b, the age-55 datum from which the date of the contact is calculated
sources: Plutarch, Moralia 785b, verified verbatim via Thayer/Penelope
Wikipedia, 'Sophocles', for the birth date of c. 497/496

stops.name: Athens, the ten talents
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction, and a late one. Plutarch transmits it citing the fourth-century historian Diyllus, now lost; Anytus is sometimes named as proposer. No inscription, decree or contemporary record survives, and the sum is treated in the scholarship as inflated legend. What sits underneath the anecdote, that the work was performed publicly in Athens, is separately probable on other grounds. Date orders the segment and rests on nothing.
stops.campa: The tradition says the assembly voted him ten talents on the motion of a citizen named Anytus, after a public reading of the work. Ten talents is a warship and its crew for a year. No decree survives, no stone, no contemporary notice; the writer who reports it is working five centuries later from a fourth-century source that is itself now lost. Underneath the figure sits a plainer claim, that the book was read aloud in Athens and Athens heard what was in it about Athens. That one is probable on other grounds. The ten talents are not.
suggested_refs: Diyllus, cited by Plutarch, the lost fourth-century source for the ten-talent decree
sources: Plutarch citing Diyllus, per secondary scholarly summary

stops.name: Thurii, the second war catches up with the book
stops.date_confidence: The internal evidence is attested: passages presuppose events after 431, including early Spartan invasions of Attica and the fate of Plataea, so the text was still being worked on into the opening years of the Peloponnesian War. The finishing horizon of about 425 is a conventional scholarly estimate from the latest datable allusion, not a record of anything. The nine-book Muse division is a Hellenistic editorial arrangement and is not demonstrably his; no autograph survives and the earliest substantial papyri postdate him by centuries. The pin is Thurii for want of any evidence of where the revision happened.
stops.campa: He is writing about a war fought before he was old enough to remember it, and while he writes, a second one starts. Passages in the finished text know things that had not happened in 431: Spartans in Attica, the end of Plataea. So the book was still open in his hands well into the new war, and it stops somewhere around 425 because that is where the latest thing it mentions stops. The nine books and their nine Muses are not his; Alexandrian editors put those on afterwards. No copy in his own hand survives.
suggested_refs: Hude's Oxford Classical Text of 1908 and N. G. Wilson's replacement Oxford edition of 2015, the current critical texts of a work with no autograph
sources: Herodotus, Histories, internal allusions post-431, per modern scholarly consensus

stops.name: Thurii, the tomb in the market place
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. The tradition is confirmed verbatim in Suda eta 536: 'after he died there he was buried in the agora. But some say that he died in Pella.' The Suda, not Marcellinus, is the source for the Thurii agora tomb; Marcellinus gives the Athens version. No grave has been securely excavated or identified anywhere. The death date of about 425 is conventional and is derived from the latest datable allusion in the work, not from any record of a death. World History Encyclopedia, fetched directly, reports a rival view that he died in Athens of the plague that killed Pericles, sometime between 425 and 413; the working notes reversed that range to 429-425 and that misquotation is not carried here.
stops.campa: The Byzantine entry says he died at Thurii and was buried in the market place, which is where a colony puts a founder or a benefactor rather than a resident who happened to die there. The date usually printed, around 425, is not a record of a death; it is the last date the book itself can be shown to know about, worked backwards into a lifespan. No grave anywhere has been dug up with his name on it. Then, in the very next clause of the same sentence, the entry says that some say he died at Pella.
stops.quote: after he died there he was buried in the agora. But some say that he died in Pella.
stops.quote_source: Suda, entry eta 536, via Suda On Line
suggested_refs: Suda eta 536, which records two incompatible deaths in one sentence and chooses neither
sources: Suda, entry eta 536, via Suda On Line

stops.name: Pella, the other grave
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction, and the weakest of the three burial claims. It survives as a single clause in the Suda with no supporting narrative, no informant, no date and no circumstance. It is recorded here because the corpus rule is that a contradiction is flagged rather than resolved, and dropping the weakest of three claims would be resolving it silently. The date is an ordering device.
stops.campa: The alternative is one clause long and arrives with nothing attached to it: some say he died at Pella. No circumstance, no informant, no date, no reason given for a man of Thurii to be in Macedon at the end of his life, and no narrative anywhere that would put him on that road. It is the weakest of the three burial claims, and it survives for the reason the other two do: a compiler who found more than one version in front of him copied out all of them instead of choosing. The Macedonian capital is four hundred miles from the Athens of the second claim and six hundred from the Italian colony of the first.
suggested_refs: Suda eta 536, the single clause that is the whole of the Pella tradition
sources: Suda, entry eta 536, via Suda On Line

stops.name: Athens, the grave beside Thucydides
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction, from Marcellinus's Life of Thucydides, late antiquity, which associates Herodotus's burial with the family tomb of Thucydides at Athens. Likely a symbolic pairing of the two historians rather than a topographical claim; the coordinates approximate the Kerameikos and Melitides Gate area where such tombs were sited and identify no grave. The related anecdote of the boy Thucydides weeping at a recitation is later still, elaborated by Photius in the ninth century and Tzetzes in the twelfth on Suda-era material. Three incompatible burial traditions stand: Thurii, Pella, Athens. The multiplicity is the historical fact and this file resolves none of it.
stops.campa: The third claim puts him in the ground at Athens, in the family plot of Thucydides. The same late body of story has the young Thucydides weep at hearing him recite, and Herodotus telling the boy's father that his son's soul yearns for knowledge. Two men who wrote the two halves of the fifth century, made into master and pupil by writers of much later centuries, and then, by one of those writers, laid in the same tomb. No burial of Herodotus has ever been identified at Athens, or at Pella, or at Thurii, or anywhere.
suggested_refs: Marcellinus, Life of Thucydides, the sole authority for the Athenian burial
Ptolemaeus Chennus via Photius, Bibliotheca, naming Plesirrhous the Thessalian as heir, the only ancient notice of any partner or household
sources: Marcellinus, Life of Thucydides, per Wikipedia 'Herodotus'
